title: Designing walkable streets: Exploring nonlinear effects of street-level built environment on older adults’ walking intention
abstract: The growing trend of older adults aging in their long-term residential settings has increased the demand for built environment designs that promote mobility, safety, and social engagement. Streets, as accessible and ubiquitous public spaces, play a critical role in shaping older adults’ walking intention and overall well-being, highlighting the importance of age-friendly street design. However, the relationship between the street-level built environment and older adults’ walking intention remains underexplored, especially regarding potential nonlinear effects. This study employed the DeepLabV3 semantic segmentation model to extract street-level built environment features from street view images. Older adults’ walking intention was quantitatively assessed by applying the Microsoft TrueSkill algorithm to convert pairwise image comparisons into ranked scores. Integrating a Gradient Boosting Decision Tree model with SHAP analysis, we examined the nonlinear and interaction effects of street-level built environment features on walking intention. Results showed that: (1) street-level built environment features were stronger determinants of older adults’ walking intention than socioeconomic factors, with green view index exerting the greatest influence; (2) the effects of street-level features exhibited nonlinear patterns, mainly power or exponential functions, with a threshold at GVI = 0.48 beyond which marginal gains diminished; (3) GVI, pedestrian path ratio, and colour richness were positively correlated with older adults’ walking intention, while building-to-street ratio, proportion of walls, and crowd concentration index showed negative correlations; and (4) significant interaction effects were observed among street-level built environment features. This study advances theoretical understanding of how microscale built environment shapes human behavior through nonlinear and synergistic mechanisms, providing actionable insights for designing age-friendly and walkable communities.

title: AI Intervention for social exclusion: the emotional regulation function and basic need satisfaction mechanism of chatbots
abstract: This study investigates how chatbot interaction affects the basic needs of individuals experiencing social exclusion, the mediating role of positive emotions, and the optimal level of linguistic anthropomorphism in chatbots. This study was conducted through three progressive experiments. Study 1 employed the Cyberball paradigm to induce social exclusion, and the results showed that excluded individuals had a significantly higher willingness to use chatbots. Study 2 combined the O-Cam paradigm, physiological indicators, and scale measurements, confirming that chatbot use could significantly enhance basic needs such as belongingness and self-esteem, as well as positive emotions, while reducing negative emotions. Among these relationships, positive emotions played a full mediating role. Study 3 set up three groups with low, medium, and high levels of linguistic anthropomorphism. The results indicated that chatbots with a medium level of anthropomorphism achieved the optimal effects in improving basic needs, enhancing positive emotions, and reducing negative emotions. Collectively, these findings indicate that chatbots can serve as effective intervention tools for social exclusion, with their mechanisms of action related to the mediation of positive emotions and moderate anthropomorphism. This research provides theoretical and practical implications for relevant psychological interventions.

title: A human-centric approach for responding to online soft hate speech: the effect of AI-based persuasion on the comment modification intention of commenters
abstract: The development of digital technology has facilitated the 'democratisation' of the internet, but it has also provided opportunities for online hate speech, which can have negative effects on individuals, groups, and society. Therefore, addressing online hate speech is crucial. However, owing to the paradox between free speech and the regulation of hate speech, soft hate speech, which is morally unacceptable but not directly constrained by law, as hard hate speech is, can result in harmful consequences in more subtle forms. In response, this study proposes shifting the focus of online hate speech research to individuals, with the objective of influencing the comment modification intention of soft hate speech commenters through AI-based persuasion and its associated strategies. Specifically, Study 1 establishes baseline effects by comparing AI-based persuasion against no-persuasion and irrelevant-persuasion controls. A pilot study examines how participant perspective moderates strategy effectiveness, providing the empirical basis for Study 2’s design. Study 2 further examines the comparative effects of emotional labelling and reason-explanation strategies and the mediating role of perceived persuasiveness under higher ecological validity conditions. In summary, this study explores a human-centric approach to responding to online soft hate speech and, through controlled scenario-based experiments, provides preliminary evidence that AI-based persuasion has a positive effect on scenario-based comment modification intention, with perceived persuasiveness identified as a psychological mechanism underlying this effect.

title: Does AI literacy enhance employee work engagement by boosting work self-efficacy or reducing job burnout? A one-year longitudinal study
abstract: In the AI era, the importance of AI literacy has become increasingly prominent, particularly among employees. Although preliminary research suggests that AI use may enhance employee work engagement, the relationship between AI literacy and work engagement remains underexplored—especially its longitudinal effects and underlying mechanisms. We conducted a one-year longitudinal study consisting of three waves of surveys with a sample of 1,108 employees aged between 21 and 60 years. At Time 1 (T1, baseline), we measured demographic information, AI literacy, and work engagement; at Time 2 (T2, 6 months later), we assessed work self-efficacy and job burnout; and at Time 3 (T3, 1 year later), we re-evaluated work engagement. Results showed that, after controlling for gender, age, AI use intensity, and T1 work engagement, T1 AI literacy significantly and positively predicted T3 work engagement. When mediators were included, T1 AI literacy not only directly predicted T3 work engagement but also exerted indirect effects through three pathways: (1) the independent mediating effect of T2 work self-efficacy, (2) the independent mediating effect of T2 job burnout, and (3) the chain mediation of T2 work self-efficacy and T2 job burnout. These findings confirm the long-term predictive role of AI literacy on work engagement and clarify the complex mechanisms behind its sustained influence, offering practical insights for organizations and individuals to better leverage AI for career development.

title: Does public transport fare discount policy affect travel choices of the elderly? An empirical study based on Chongqing, China
abstract: As population aging accelerates, public transport fare discounts have become a crucial tool for cities to address the mobility needs of the elderly. This study aims to optimize such policies by examining the psychological decision-making process of elderly bus users, using survey data from Chongqing, China, collected in 2022 ( N = 556) and validated with a second cross-sectional survey conducted in 2026 ( N = 174). It investigates how socioeconomic characteristics and subjective attitudes influence travel decisions under different discount scenarios. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) is applied to confirm the impact paths of elderly transit policy acceptance, bus travel dependency, and discount schemes on travel mode choice. In addition, Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT) are employed to explore the non-linear interactions among individual attributes and subjective attitudes in the context of varying discount scenarios. The results reveal that higher discount rates significantly encourage elderly individuals to choose public transport. Bus travel dependency emerges as the most robust predictor of mode choice, validated across both survey waves. The older elderly (over 75 years) show higher sensitivity to discounts despite lower baseline travel willingness. Furthermore, discount policies have a stronger incentive effect on groups with non-rigid travel demands. The findings suggest that tailored discount strategies, combined with enhanced service quality and targeted policy promotion, can increase public transport use among the elderly. Such refinements are expected to improve social participation, enhance quality of life, and provide empirical guidance for optimizing elderly bus fare discount policies.

title: I deserve rewards! Exploring the effect of employees’ reputation for effective AI usage on turnover intention
abstract: Although existing research generally acknowledges the positive effects of general reputation, this study argues that prior research has overstated the benefits of reputation while neglecting its potential drawbacks. We introduce a domain-specific reputation—employees’ reputation for effective AI usage, referring to positive evaluations of an individual’s ability to effectively use AI by others. Based on the social comparison theory, this research examines the negative effects of employees’ reputation for effective AI usage. The findings from both an experiment and a three-wave study reveal that employees’ reputation for effective AI usage is positively associated with turnover intention through psychological entitlement. Moreover, we identify rewards for effective AI usage as an essential boundary condition. Specifically, the positive relationship between employees’ reputation for effective AI usage and psychological entitlement and the indirect impact of employees’ reputation for effective AI usage on turnover intention through psychological entitlement are weaker when rewards for effective AI usage are high. The study also explores theoretical and practical implications, as well as outlines future research directions.

title: Sentiment analysis in rural areas: a systematic review of applications and approaches
abstract: Rural depopulation and territorial imbalances are ongoing challenges that require innovative tools for understanding community needs and informing evidence-based policy. Sentiment Analysis (SA) has emerged as a promising methodology for extracting emotional information from large volumes of digital text data. However, despite its growing methodological relevance across the social sciences, its application to rural contexts is limited, and no prior systematic review has examined the application of SA within rural research. This article aims to assess the usefulness and potential of SA in rural research through a systematic review of existing applications and a critical analysis of its methodological contributions. The systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies applied SA to textual or social media data and focused on rural areas or explicitly compared rural and urban contexts. Searches were performed in Scopus and Web of Science (WOS) up to March 2025. A total of 47 studies were included and analysed. Data extraction was performed from the reviewed studies, collecting information on the location, study type, authors’ discipline, and methodological quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and a consensus review by the research team. Key results were extracted, including areas of application of SA, methodologies employed, and data sources. Additionally, a thematic analysis was conducted considering the main areas of application of SA and its limitations. The studies reveal a developing field where SA is increasingly applied across various domains, particularly in rural tourism and public health, as well as in agriculture, food policy and social well-being. A significant geographic concentration of research is observed in China and the United States. The studies employ various SA processing methodologies (lexicon-based, machine learning, deep learning and hybrid approaches) and diverse data sources (social media, surveys, digital reviews). Methodological quality was generally high, with 85% of the studies scoring 7 or higher on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Furthermore, the analysis identified notable differences in perceptions between rural and urban areas, emphasizing the importance of considering local contexts in public policy discussions. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the role of SA in rural development and offer valuable insights for future research and policy formulation aimed at addressing the specific needs of rural communities.

title: Cybernetics, the Anthropocene, and education: student learning in conjunction with AI
abstract: This article develops a speculative and empirically inflected account of how university students are learning in conjunction with artificial intelligence (AI). It brings together three interlocking fields: cybernetics, the Anthropocene and education. Cybernetics is central because the communicative and control processes through which students engage AI for research, writing and study raise fundamental questions about agency, authorship and the capacity to think otherwise within machine-mediated capitalism. The Anthropocene provides a second axis of analysis, naming the planetary consequences of human technological development, economic acceleration and ecological damage. Education forms the third axis, because universities are key sites in which these cybernetic and Anthropocene dynamics are materialised through everyday practices of study, assessment and writing. The article combines philosophical analysis with empirical data from education students learning with AI. These data are organised as “data portals”: analytic thresholds that interrupt, extend and test the conceptual argument. Drawing on Deleuze’s transcendental empiricism, the article argues that students do not encounter AI as an external tool alone, but as part of a wider student-AI-university assemblage. The article concludes that agency persists in this assemblage, but is increasingly modulated by feedback, acceleration, assessment pressure, economic precarity and machinic cognition.

title: Social simulations with large language model risk Utopian illusion
abstract: Reliable simulation of human behaviour is essential for explaining, predicting, and intervening in our society. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in emulating human behaviours, interactions, and decision-making, offering a powerful new lens for social science studies. However, the extent to which LLMs diverge from authentic human behaviour in social contexts remains underexplored, posing risks of misinterpretation in scientific studies and unintended consequences in real-world applications. This study introduces a systematic framework for analysing LLMs’ behaviour in social simulation. Our approach simulates multi-agent interactions through chatroom-style conversations and analyzes them across five linguistic dimensions, providing a simple yet effective method to examine emergent social cognitive biases. We conduct extensive experiments involving eight representative LLMs across three families. The results show that LLMs do not faithfully reproduce genuine human behaviour but instead reflect overly idealised versions of it, shaped by the social desirability bias. In particular, LLMs show social role bias, primacy effect, and positivity bias, resulting in “Utopian” societies that lack the complexity and variability of real human interactions. These findings suggest that LLM-based simulations reproduce how people wish others to behave rather than how people themselves behave, a divergence that amplifies through multi-agent interaction and, if uncritically adopted in social analysis, may produce an artificially narrowed representation of social life. This paper calls for more socially grounded LLMs that better capture the diversity of human social behaviour.

title: Profiling fertility anxiety in young Chinese women: evidence from latent class and random forest analyses
abstract: Amid China’s demographic transition and evolving fertility policies, fertility anxiety among young women has attracted increasing attention. However, the multidimensional structure of fertility anxiety remains underexplored, especially with respect to systematic examinations of heterogeneity across marital and fertility statuses and the factors related to these variations. This study collected 2000 valid samples through a questionnaire survey, employed latent profile analysis to identify types of fertility anxiety, and used a random forest model to rank the importance of key influencing factors. The results show that multiple types exist within each marital and fertility status group, and that emotional anxiety has significantly greater discriminative power than cognitive anxiety. Parenting sense of competence, marital quality, perceived social fairness, and social support were identified as core predictive variables. The sources of moderate-to-high anxiety were manifested in actual parenting stress, decision-making uncertainty, and future identity expectations, respectively. The classification accuracy and confusion matrix results indicate that the model demonstrates high robustness in distinguishing fertility anxiety profiles across different marital and fertility statuses. The findings indicate that fertility anxiety is a multidimensional, context-dependent psychological structure jointly shaped by cultural norms, resource adequacy, and relational support. At the policy level, China should adopt differentiated strategies: enhancing parenting competence and childcare service provision, strengthening marital stability and fertility counseling, alleviating gendered role pressures, and improving perceptions of fairness. At the international level, low-fertility countries should tailor support measures to local gender norms and welfare systems, prioritizing the development of emotional regulation interventions and family–work-friendly policies to effectively reduce fertility anxiety and promote overall well-being.

title: China’s cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zones: emission reduction and spatial spillover effects on air quality
abstract: Cross-border e-commerce (CBEC) is currently the fastest-growing and most promising new trade format, acting as a pivotal engine for transforming and upgrading China’s foreign trade. While the rapid expansion of CBEC has profoundly impacted the economy, its potential environmental externalities remain underexplored. Based on panel data from 276 prefecture-level cities in China spanning 2010 to 2022, this study treats the phased implementation of the Cross-border e-commerce Comprehensive Pilot Zone (CPZ) policy as a quasi-natural experiment. By employing multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) and spatial econometric models, we evaluate the impact of the CPZ policy on PM2.5 concentrations in both pilot cities and their neighboring areas. The findings reveal that: (1) The CPZ policy significantly reduces PM2.5 concentrations in pilot cities, a conclusion that remains consistent across multiple robustness tests, including alternative indicators, instrumental variables, PSM-DID, and double machine learning. (2) The emission reduction effect is more pronounced in resource-based cities and non-environmental priority cities. (3) The CPZ generates emission reduction spillover effects on surrounding cities within a 0–300 km radius, primarily transmitted through channels involving spatially diffusive green technological innovation, digital technological innovation, and energy consumption intensity. Based on these findings, the following policy implications are derived: (1) Continuously promote the high-quality development of CPZs and strengthen the green development orientation. (2) Formulate region-specific and differentiated policies based on local conditions. (3) Enhance regional coordination and technology spillover mechanisms. (4) Build a dual-drive system integrating green technology and digital technology.

title: Advancing generative AI for stakeholder empowerment in community-based tourism: an experimental approach to inclusivity and sustainability
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming community-based tourism (CBT) by promoting inclusivity and sustainability. This study investigates the use of Kimi.ai, a GenAI platform developed by Moonshot AI, to simulate interactions among six key stakeholder groups: administrators, investors, entrepreneurs, local business owners, marginalized residents, and tourists. The findings demonstrate that identity-based chatbot interactions effectively address stakeholder-specific needs, support cultural preservation, and encourage economic inclusivity. Through thematic and sentiment analyses, the study shows GenAI’s potential to enhance stakeholder engagement, resource coordination, and problem-solving within Community-Based Tourism ecosystems. It offers practical insights for policymakers and practitioners, highlighting GenAI’s role in advancing equitable and sustainable tourism. Future research on emerging technologies is encouraged to further strengthen decision-making and operational effectiveness in community-based tourism development.

title: The effects of artificial intelligence and environmental pollution on green growth in China
abstract: Achieving sustainable economic development requires policies that reconcile growth with environmental protection. This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and environmental regulation (ER) affect green growth (GG) in China, controlling for fiscal policy, human capital and urbanization. Using panel data for 30 provinces over 2011–2020, we construct a composite GG index with the entropy method and estimate effects with the Method of Moments Quantile Regression (MMQR), complemented by a panel quantile Granger causality test. AI and ER both raise GG at the lower, middle and upper quantiles. The AI effect grows across quantiles, while the ER effect is small and declines slightly. Fiscal policy, human capital and urbanization also promote GG, and linear panel estimates confirm these results. The AI effect depends on adoption level: it is positive in high-AI provinces but negative in low-AI provinces. The causality test indicates that all five variables Granger-cause GG across most quantiles. These findings support combining AI adoption with environmental regulation, alongside targeted support for low-adoption provinces.

title: “Creatures of the symbolic ocean”: toward a structure-mapped apperception of synthetic cognition
abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models has triggered a global policy dilemma regarding anthropomorphism and user dependency. Because this regulatory challenge is closely tied to an unresolved conceptual ambiguity concerning the nature of AI, this article introduces a phenomenological framework to delineate the essential character of synthetic cognition. To this end, we demonstrate a functional isomorphism between the generative logic of human consciousness and the computational operations of LLMs. Specifically, we align human hyletic processing, representation integration, and recursive reflection with the model mechanisms of loss-driven token embedding, Attention-FFN synthesis, and recursive policy emergence. Synthesizing these functional parallels, we propose “Structure-Mapped Apperception” to conceptualize LLMs as “Creatures of the Symbolic Ocean” navigating semantic currents. Crucially, this same apperceptive lens delineates the fundamental existential gaps that separate current AI from embodied subjectivity, revealing these systems to be existentially suspended. Ultimately, this heuristic offers a philosophical basis for AI governance by providing a conceptual framework to mitigate psychological harm and data-polluting sycophancy.

title: From appropriate use to dependency: How AI attitude and use motivations shape university students’ AI dependency
abstract: Abstract Whether students develop dependence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies largely depends on their attitudes toward using such tools. Existing studies have primarily explained the formation of AI dependence from the perspectives of usage attitudes and technological characteristics, while paying limited attention to the psychological mechanisms through which attitudes exert their influence. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the present study examines how different types of use motivation mediate the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and AI dependence. A total of 405 university students completed a comprehensive questionnaire measuring AI attitudes, use motivations, and AI dependence. The results indicate that: (i) AI attitudes do not directly predict AI dependence; instead, their effects are transmitted through multiple motivational pathways, with intrinsic motivation inhibiting AI dependence, whereas identified regulation facilitates its development; (ii) three distinct AI dependence profiles were identified: dependent, moderate, and conservative users. These profiles exhibited clear stratification, with dependent users showing the highest scores across all dimensions and conservative users the lowest; and (iii) individuals with stronger motivations are more likely to be classified into the dependent user profile, with external motivation playing a particularly salient role. These findings enrich the literature on AI technology dependence and offer practical implications for higher education administrators, tool developers, and educational researchers.

title: Decoding urban thermal well-being: bridging the gap between physical cooling and social perception in wetlands via AI-enhanced sensing
abstract: Abstract Urban wetland parks serve as vital infrastructure for climate resilience, yet a critical epistemological gap remains between their objective thermodynamic performance and the subjective thermal well-being of visitors. To bridge this divide, this study establishes an integrated computational social science framework that couples remote sensing metrics with AI-decoded digital narratives. Focusing on the high-density context of Shenzhen, we synthesized Landsat-derived environmental data with large-scale crowd-sourced digital footprints, employing Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract in-situ thermal sentiments from 11,109 online reviews. The analysis suggests that human thermal experience may follow non-linear trajectories relative to physical indicators. Patch Richness Density (PRD) was strongly associated with cooling efficiency, suggesting that landscape heterogeneity may enhance thermal well-being through both physical air exchange and the psychological benefits of visual complexity. The study further identifies a counter-intuitive “accessibility paradox”: a moderate density of impervious-surface patches (PD-I) is associated with higher “cool” perception, with an exploratory empirical turning point around 32.3 n/ha in the Shenzhen wetland-park sample. This pattern suggests that well-distributed access infrastructure may act as a behavioral mediator, facilitating visitor access to cooling cores while remaining subject to site-specific ecological and urban-morphological conditions. Additionally, comfortable perception shows an empirical turning point around a Land Surface Temperature (LST) of 28.8 °C, indicating a context-dependent adaptation range rather than a universal comfort standard. These findings challenge the conventional “minimize-pavement” assumption and suggest that thermal satisfaction depends on a strategic balance between ecological integrity and recreational accessibility. Rather than providing prescriptive design benchmarks, the identified non-linear patterns offer hypothesis-generating evidence and indicative design references for human-centric urban governance. This study contributes a replicable, AI-enhanced paradigm for aligning climate resilience research with public thermal perception.

title: Embedding far transfer in higher education: A fractal systems model for adaptive expertise and equity in STEM learning
abstract: STEM-focused higher education systems worldwide face increasing pressure to prepare learners for complex, ill-structured challenges, from climate resilience to AI ethics, that demand adaptive expertise and integrative thinking. Yet most higher education environments remain oriented toward near transfer, emphasizing the application of knowledge within familiar boundaries more consistently than flexible reasoning across diverse contexts. This essay advances the Fractal Systems Model (FSM), an equity-centered conceptual framework that integrates cognitive, sociocultural, and systems-theoretical perspectives to examine how higher education systems might be designed to support adaptive expertise. FSM reconceptualizes far transfer as a potentially designable system property shaped by recursively aligned learning processes across educational scales. Drawing on research in cognitive science, situated learning, equity studies, and Discipline-Based Education Research, the model specifies how opportunities for abstraction, integration, and recontextualization can recur across the micro, meso, and macro levels of higher education. FSM further proposes that alignment across these levels may strengthen opportunities for far transfer and adaptive expertise while reducing reliance on isolated courses or selective enrichment experiences. The model offers researchers, practitioners, and policymakers an empirically testable systems framework for examining how equitable learning ecosystems can be designed to support adaptive expertise for the complex challenges of the twenty-first century.

title: Spatial differentiation and driving mechanisms of Tibetan and Qiang traditional villages in northwestern Sichuan, China
abstract: Abstract Northwestern Sichuan Province in China, characterized by its unique geography and rich ethnic culture, hosts numerous Tibetan–Qiang Traditional Villages (TTVNS) of significant conservation value. These villages exhibit pronounced macro-level spatial inequalities, making the study of their spatial differentiation and the quantification of driving mechanisms essential for implementing targeted conservation strategies. This study examines 412 TTVNS using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE), accessibility-based clustering, Optimal Parameter Geographical Detector (OPGD), Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR), and Random Forest with SHAP (RF–SHAP) to identify spatial patterns and quantify the mechanisms influencing them. The results indicate that: (1) TTVNS display a “multi-core clustering with contiguous distribution” pattern, forming two northeast–southwest aggregation belts, with significant positive spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I = 0.175); (2) in single-factor detection, Cultivated Land (X3, q = 0.3019), Population (X19, q = 0.2510), and Road Density (X13, q = 0.2303) are the strongest explanatory factors, while the strongest interaction occurs between Temperature (X9) and Population (X19, q = 0.406), demonstrating that spatial differentiation is driven by the coupling of environmental suitability and social support rather than any single factor; (3) model comparison shows that MGWR substantially outperforms OLS and GWR, with R² increasing from 0.3049 and 0.3246 to 0.6568, confirming pronounced spatial non-stationarity in the driving mechanisms of TTVNS; (4) different categories of drivers exhibit distinct pathways: nature and geography influence aggregation through cultivated land, river systems, and temperature; location and transportation shape a “node–corridor” settlement pattern along valley corridors; humanities and religion affect clustering through the coupling of religious nodes and local social structures; society and economy reshape contemporary spatial patterns primarily via tourism development and population dynamics. These findings demonstrate that the spatial differentiation of TTVNS emerges under long-term natural constraints and religious-cultural networks, and continues to be reshaped by modern transportation and tourism development. The study provides a quantitative basis for designing differentiated and context-specific conservation strategies.

title: Research on the impact of artificial intelligence on the pollution governance mechanism and pathways in border regions
abstract: Abstract Boundary pollution poses obstacles to environmental governance and industrial upgrading, while traditional monitoring methods fail to provide a fundamental solution. Drawing on data from boundary prefecture-level cities between 2016 and 2022, this paper delves into the governance effect of artificial intelligence (AI) on boundary pollution. The research reveals that AI significantly improves the situation of boundary pollution, breaking down market segmentation, enhancing supervision, and addressing negative externalities through positive spillover effects. Furthermore, the development of AI suppresses pollution in adjacent regions through economic ties, mitigating the negative impact of competition among local governments. This suppressive effect is particularly pronounced in regions with low levels of regional collaboration and contiguous poverty-stricken regions. Consequently, the government should attach great importance to the role of digital technology in boundary pollution control, strengthen cooperation with the market, foster regional economic ties, and promote green and high-quality economic development in boundary regions, ultimately achieving sustainable development goals.

title: From narrative generation to interpretive stabilization: generative AI and the mechanism of ethical understanding
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly reshaping narrative practices through character monologues and emotionally guided storytelling on digital platforms such as Bilibili and Chinese TikTok. While existing AI ethics scholarship has primarily focused on issues of bias, transparency, and governance, it offers limited explanatory power for understanding how generative systems reorganize the interpretive conditions under which moral judgment is formed. To address this gap, this study develops Generative Interpretive Mediation (GIM) as a mechanism-based framework for analyzing how GenAI intervenes in interpretive processes prior to explicit ethical evaluation. Based on an interpretive research design, the article examines widely circulated AI-generated character monologues as analytically selected cases of platform-mediated narrative production. The analysis identifies three interrelated operations: interpretive selection, interpretive pre-structuring, and interpretive orientation. Together, these operations do not simply produce narratives, but stabilize interpretation by reducing narrative ambiguity and guiding users toward coherent psychological trajectories. In doing so, GenAI often replaces sustained interpretive effort with pre-shaped explanatory closure, thereby reshaping how understanding is formed in everyday engagement with digital narratives. By bringing narrative hermeneutics into dialogue with behavioral accounts of the “illusion of understanding” and “decisional inertia,” the article situates GIM within an emerging epistemic turn in AI ethics. It argues that the central ethical concern of GenAI lies not primarily in biased outputs, but in its capacity to reorganize interpretive environments in ways that subtly condition the formation of public moral judgment.

title: Mapping interdependencies among challenges to artificial intelligence adoption in drug discovery
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) offers significant potential to accelerate drug discovery, yet its adoption remains constrained by interdependent technical, organizational, and regulatory barriers. This study applies Fuzzy DEMATEL to analyze twelve challenges and uncover their causal structure using expert judgments expressed as triangular fuzzy numbers. Following normalization and CFCS defuzzification, Resistance to Change, Lack of Standardization, Limited Trust in AI Outputs, Talent Shortage, and Lack of Clinical Validation emerge as the primary causal drivers. These upstream barriers exert strong influence on downstream effects, including Regulatory Barriers, Biological Complexity, Integration with Legacy Systems, and Poor Data Quality. The findings indicate that several constraints commonly viewed as external are, in practice, manifestations of internal organizational and technical shortcomings. By providing a structured causal prioritization of barriers, this study offers actionable guidance for targeting high-leverage interventions in AI-enabled drug discovery. Findings reflect expert judgment within a North Cyprus context and should be interpreted as indicative organizational signals rather than universal prescriptions.

title: How balance, contour, symmetry, and complexity predict the perceived emotions in Chinese traditional music
abstract: Understanding how musical structure shapes emotion perception remains a central question in music psychology, yet the role of mid-level structural features in Chinese traditional music is underexplored. This study investigated how balance, contour, symmetry, and complexity (BCSC framework) predict perceived emotions in Chinese traditional music using both linear (Lasso-selected multiple regression) and nonlinear (random forest regression) modeling approaches. Analyses included dimensional emotions (valence, arousal) and seven discrete emotions (anger, gentleness, happiness, peacefulness, sadness, solemnness, transcendence). Linear regressions showed that BCSC features explained 35.1% of variance in valence and 37.1% in arousal. For valence, Total Asymmetry (β = 0.266, p < 0.001), Average Local First-Order Entropy (β = 0.862, p < 0.001), Third-Order Duration Entropy (β = 0.511, p = 0.022), and Event Density (β = −0.890, p < 0.001) were among the strongest predictors. For arousal, Duration Abruptness, Total Asymmetry, Average Local First-Order Entropy, and Third-Order Duration Entropy were significant positive predictors (all ps < 0.01), while Rhythmic Abruptness, Event Density, and First-Order Duration Entropy showed significant negative effects (all ps < 0.001). For discrete emotions, predictive power ranged from adjusted R² = 0.157 (peacefulness) to 0.386 (happiness), with emotion-specific patterns: e.g., Bi-Unbalance (β = 0.316, p < 0.001) predicted anger, while First-Order Duration Entropy had opposing effects for anger (β = −0.252, p < 0.001) and peacefulness (β = 0.403, p < 0.001). Nonlinear models confirmed feature importance patterns, highlighting the roles of temporal irregularity, melodic interval size, and structural imbalance. Overall, these findings demonstrate that mid-level structural features provide systematic elements that serve as emotional cues for perceived emotions in Chinese traditional music.

title: Data is not knowledge: Hayek’s epistemological challenge to artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is routinely described as a knowledge technology. This paper argues that the description misplaces a boundary Hayek drew in 1945, between “scientific knowledge”—codifiable, statistical, articulable—and “knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place.” Kiesling (2015) reconstructs part of the latter as the contextual knowledge problem: knowledge that does not exist outside the interaction producing it, as against the complexity problem of aggregating knowledge that exists dispersed but can in principle be codified. The reconstruction is interpretive and identifies a generative subset of Hayek’s category rather than its whole content; much of the remainder is knowledge agents already possess, and AI dissolves a good deal of it. The argument is not that machine systems cannot discover novel alternatives, nor that their search spaces are closed; both are conceded. It is that discovering means does not originate the ultimate ends by reference to which alternatives acquire economic significance, and that current systems receive those ends rather than constituting them. Under a Misesian account of evaluative agency—a premise the paper declares rather than derives—better aggregation, prediction and optimisation therefore cannot by themselves resolve the generative subset, so neither Polanyian tacit knowledge in large language models nor microstructure price discovery by high-frequency traders reaches it. The taxonomy is applied at three levels—the data pipeline, the tacit-knowledge debate, and the institutional conditions of price generation—as three applications of one classification rather than three independent demonstrations. Its products are a set of operational tests, none of which has been run and which are here read against a published Q-learning pricing architecture, and a criterion distinguishing context-preserving from context-suppressing deployment at the level of the market.

title: Demand structure transition, policy interventions and China’s grain security: A DSGE-based investigation of self-sufficiency dynamics
abstract: Confronted with the transformation of grain demand structure and the risks of short-term demand surges induced by the upgrading of residents’ dietary patterns, as well as the frequent occurrence of geopolitical conflicts and natural disasters, how to stabilize the grain self-sufficiency rate through precise policy interventions has emerged as a pivotal issue in China’s grain security governance. This study first employs the random forest approach for variable selection. On this basis, we construct a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model comprising heterogeneous households (farm households and general households) and multiple production sectors (staple food, soybean, and non-grain sectors). The model systematically incorporates a total of seven categories of exogenous shocks: demand shocks for staple food and soybean, production technology shocks for the two grain types, production subsidy shocks, and agricultural machinery purchase subsidy shocks for farm households. Simulation analysis reveals that: (1) Sudden demand shocks are the primary factor driving short-term fluctuations in grain prices and affecting the real purchasing power of residents, while also eroding grain self-sufficiency rate; (2) Production technology shocks represent the fundamental force underlying the long-term evolution of grain output and self-sufficiency rate. Positive technology shocks can significantly raise the grain self-sufficiency rate and improve residents’ consumption welfare, which highlights the core role of technological progress in safeguarding national grain security. (3) Both production subsidies and agricultural machinery purchase subsidies are effective in coping with external shocks. The former delivers direct and rapid effects in stabilizing grain output and ensuring supply in the short run, whereas the latter focuses more on enhancing systemic resilience through long-term capital accumulation. The two policies are heterogeneous in terms of their mechanism and time effectiveness. This study provides a dynamic quantitative basis for optimizing the agricultural support policy system and systematically enhancing grain security capacity in a complex and volatile domestic and international environment.

title: Decomposing the gender gap in subjective well-being: evidence from a machine learning-based switching framework
abstract: Human well-being has received increasing attention as an indicator of individual and social health and as a consideration in public policy. Gender differences in subjective well-being (SWB), a widely accepted indicator of human well-being, have long been documented. However, explanations of these gender differences remain varied and inconclusive. This study utilizes Gallup World Poll data comprising 1,911,212 observations from 2009 to 2022. Employing advanced machine-learning techniques within an Exogenous Switching Treatment Effect Model (ESTEM) framework, we decompose the gender gap in SWB into differences in characteristics and differences in regime-specific returns. Conditional on observed characteristics and under a common predictive regime, the model predicts higher SWB for men. In contrast, the regime-specific returns component is associated with lower predicted well-being under the male regime. This component also increases over time, widening the estimated gender gap in SWB, while its magnitude varies across countries. The results suggest the potential relevance of institutional flexibility and reduced gender-role pressures for addressing gender disparities in human well-being.

title: Belief to behavior: how AI self-efficacy shapes AI acceptance through AI literacy
abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into higher education has raised important questions regarding students’ acceptance of AI and the psychological and cognitive factors shaping their engagement with these systems. This study aimed to examine how university students’ AI self-efficacy influences their acceptance of AI, whether AI literacy helps explain this relationship, and whether greater AI acceptance is associated with lower AI anxiety. For the present study, data were obtained from 622 undergraduate students at a public university. Empirical analyses were based on validated scales measuring AI self-efficacy, AI literacy, AI acceptance, and AI anxiety, and conducted using correlation analyses and regression-based mediation models via the PROCESS Macro. The results showed that AI self-efficacy was positively associated with AI acceptance, both directly and indirectly through AI literacy. Higher AI acceptance was also associated with lower AI anxiety; however, this relationship should not be interpreted as causal. These findings support a sequential motivational, cognitive and affective model of AI engagement and highlight the importance of integrating confidence-building interventions with literacy-focused instructional strategies to promote psychologically adaptive and sustainable AI integration in higher education contexts.

title: The impact of the data factor platform on the urban green innovation: evidence from China
abstract: Abstract With the rapid expansion of the digital economy, data elements have emerged as a pivotal force shaping urban green development. This study offers a novel perspective by examining how the construction of data factor platform influences urban green innovation. From the channel of artificial intelligence (AI) development and human capital accumulation, we propose a mechanism framework. Based on the city-level data from 2010 to 2022 in China, using the multi-period Difference-in-Difference (DID) model, we explore the impact of the data factor platform construction on urban green innovation. The results reveal that data factor platform construction can stimulate urban green innovation. The data factor platform construction stimulates urban green innovation through the channel of promoting AI development and accelerating human capital accumulation. The impact of the data factor platform construction on the urban green innovation is heterogeneous. The data factor platform construction has a larger effect on the urban green innovation in the low-carbon pilot city situation and cities with larger economic scales. The further analysis results reveal that the data factor platform construction in the surrounding areas effectively promotes local green innovation. According to the above conclusions, in the green transition process, the government should pay attention to data factor platform programs and make a combination of policies to stimulate green innovations.

title: Cognitive mechanisms of AI agent behavioral intention among design graduate students: an integrated TAM–TTF perspective
abstract: AI agents are reshaping educational systems and transforming teaching and learning in design disciplines. However, the psychological mechanisms underlying AI-agent use among design graduate students remain underexplored, as does the interaction between design-specific tasks and AI agents. To address this gap, this study integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Task–Technology Fit (TTF) theory to explain how technological cognition and task-fit perceptions jointly shape behavioral intention to use AI agents. Because conventional structural modeling mainly captures hypothesized linear relationships, MLP-ANN was added to assess nonlinear patterns and predictor importance. Using 405 valid questionnaire responses, the model was tested through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), a Multilayer Perceptron Artificial Neural Network (MLP-ANN), and Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA). PLS-SEM supported nine of ten hypotheses. Self-efficacy positively affected perceived usefulness (β = 0.458, p < 0.001) and perceived ease of use (β = 0.394, p < 0.001). Perceived enjoyment enhanced perceived ease of use (β = 0.220, p < 0.001), but its effect on perceived usefulness was negative and nonsignificant (β = −0.033, p = 0.483). Perceived usefulness (β = 0.376, p < 0.001), perceived ease of use (β = 0.185, p < 0.001), and task–technology fit (β = 0.224, p < 0.001) positively influenced attitude. Task characteristics (β = 0.322, p < 0.001) and technology characteristics (β = 0.266, p < 0.001) positively affected task–technology fit, while attitude promoted behavioral intention (β = 0.388, p < 0.001). Ten-fold cross-validated MLP-ANN models produced mean RMSE values of 0.3263–0.4203 across training and testing and broadly confirmed the PLS-SEM predictor-importance patterns. NCA further identified self-efficacy (d = 0.125, p = 0.015) and attitude (d = 0.132, p < 0.001) as necessary conditions for perceived usefulness and behavioral intention, respectively. This study extends the integrated TAM–TTF framework to design education and offers theoretical and practical implications for effective AI-agent use in design disciplines.
